title: Your teacher
hookLine: the value of a living teacher

lines: A STRANGER WITH NO DUST ON HIM.
cards: The companions are sitting with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when a stranger walks in. His clothes are bright white, his hair very black, and there's no dust of travel on him. Nobody knows him.
He sits so close that his knees touch the Prophet's knees, rests his hands on his thighs, and starts asking. What is Islam? What is faith?
What is excellence? After he leaves, the Prophet tells them who it was: Jibril, who came to teach you your religion. That's how Sahih Muslim tells it.

teach.h: A LESSON GIVEN KNEE TO KNEE.
teach.b: Jibril could have left a scroll. Instead, the religion was taught as a conversation between two people sitting close, with questions, answers, and witnesses who carried it on. The Qur'an travels the same way.
It's a recitation, heard and repeated. A student sits with a teacher who listens and corrects a vowel, a pause, a letter held too short.
In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet says the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it: learning and teaching in the same sentence.

teach.h: MUSA GOES LOOKING FOR A TEACHER.
teach.b: Even a prophet went looking for a teacher. In surah al-Kahf, Musa travels to find a servant of God who has been given knowledge, and asks to follow him so that he may be taught.
The man warns him he won't have the patience.
What follows is a lesson in exactly that: a student who keeps interrupting, and a teacher who bears with him twice before they part. So a teacher isn't only someone who knows more.
A teacher can see you, your mistakes, your rushing, your gaps, and say so kindly. People find one today in many ways. Some study with an imam at a local mosque.

Some join a class for women taught by a woman scholar. Some begin online and then look for a person they can sit with. Musa's own words are a good model for the asking: may I follow you, so that you teach me?

how: Muslims study with teachers in mosques, schools and homes, especially for the Qur'an, which is learned by reciting aloud to a teacher who corrects the pronunciation; some students look for a teacher whose own learning comes through a chain of teachers.

o: an imam who must approve every choice you make
a living person who learned from someone and can correct you
any book or video that explains the religion clearly

s: in the hadith of Jibril, the religion was handed over as a written scroll
Jibril sat knee to knee with the Prophet and asked questions; the companions witnessed it (Sahih Muslim).
in the Qur'an, Musa asks a servant of God to teach him
surah al-Kahf tells how Musa traveled to find him and asked to follow him and learn.
a teacher only matters if you can't read
a teacher listens and corrects, a vowel, a pause, a rushing student, which a book can't do.

games.q: you're with the companions. a stranger with no dust of travel walks in and goes straight to the Prophet. what does he do?
o: sits knee to knee and asks questions.
stands and preaches to the room.

games.why: he sat so close their knees touched and asked about Islam, faith and excellence. afterward the Prophet said it was Jibril, who came to teach you your religion (Sahih Muslim).

practice: Think of one thing you've tried to learn alone and stalled on: a surah you keep stumbling through, a question you keep meaning to settle, a skill half-learned from videos.

Picture asking someone for help with it, face to face, the way Musa asked, and quietly name what makes the asking hard, pride, shyness, not knowing whom to ask, without obeying it. If you pray, ask Allah to make the asking easier.

wordCard.voice: Your teacher. A living person who learned from someone, and can sit close enough to correct you. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a teacher, one who teaches.

carryVoice: Your line: find a teacher. Some things are only learned knee to knee. I'll be here tomorrow.
